messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 58
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Psychiatrist
  trauma_type: Life-threatening accident
  pcl5: 37

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Trauma-Related Events: Trauma-related events, Intrusive Thoughts: Unwanted thoughts, Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident
  Maladaptive Strategies: Emotion Control: I try hard to control my emotions, Avoid Sex: Sex, Avoid Sleep: Going to sleep or lying in the dark
  Threat: Startle Response: Feeling jumpy or easily startled, Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room, Waking Alert: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe
  Memory: Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, No Coherent Story: I cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to myself, Confused Sequence: I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order
  Negative Appraisals: Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse, Self-Doubt: I can't trust that I will do the right thing, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place

Vignette:
Moana Te Rangi is a 58-year-old psychiatrist who came to treatment months after a life-threatening car accident that she still cannot recount in a settled, orderly way. She is divorced and lives alone, and before the accident she had been accustomed to moving through long clinic days with composure and authority. What she remembers most clearly is not a smooth sequence but striking fragments: the sudden sight of another car where it should not have been, metal coming toward her, the impact, and the sense that she might die before anyone reached her. When she tries to tell the story, she stops and starts, correcting herself, unsure what happened first and what came after. She says there are pieces that arrive in full force and other pieces that feel missing altogether, and this inability to form a coherent account unsettles her almost as much as the crash itself.

In the weeks that followed, the accident did not remain in the past in any stable way. Instead, aspects of it seemed to return without warning. She might be driving to the hospital garage before clinic, glance across traffic, and suddenly be flooded by the image of cars colliding. At other times there is no obvious build-up at all: something in her surroundings—a particular angle of headlights, the position of two vehicles at an intersection, the abrupt movement of a car entering her field of vision—brings back the memory with a force that feels immediate rather than remembered. She describes unwanted thoughts of the accident intruding while she is writing notes between patients or sitting in case conference, as if the event has inserted itself into moments that used to belong to ordinary concentration.

These experiences have changed how she carries herself through the day. In meetings at the hospital, Moana now chooses the chair that lets her keep her back against the wall and the whole room in view. If a resident has already taken that seat, she feels tense until she can reposition herself. A door opening behind her or a sudden noise in the corridor makes her jolt visibly. She is embarrassed by how easily startled she has become, especially in professional spaces where she has long been the person others experience as calm. She has come to believe that the world is fundamentally dangerous in a way she can no longer disregard, and she no longer trusts herself to respond correctly when something happens fast. That thought has become particularly painful for her as a physician: she was once confident in her judgment, but now she hears herself wondering whether, in the crucial moment, she would do the wrong thing.

At home, nights are the hardest. Going to sleep means lying in the dark and losing the vigilance that feels necessary to stay safe, so she delays bedtime for hours, keeping lights on, reading, or scrolling on her phone until she is exhausted. Even then she wakes abruptly and checks her surroundings before she can settle again. She speaks of this not as a habit she likes but as something she feels compelled to do. During the day she tries just as strenuously to control her emotions, keeping her face composed and her voice even with patients and colleagues, as though any visible distress would confirm that she has been permanently altered for the worse. She says she is no longer the person she was before the crash, and there is grief and shame in the certainty with which she says it.

Her personal life has narrowed in quieter ways. Although divorced, she had maintained the possibility of intimacy in a later-life relationship, but since the accident she has avoided sex altogether. She does not describe this as lack of interest so much as an inability to tolerate the vulnerability of it; closeness has come to feel exposing rather than comforting. Over time, the effort of managing herself at work, scanning for safety in rooms, enduring sudden crash images, and resisting sleep has left her more isolated than she intended. She still functions at a high level, but with increasing strain, and she notices how much of each day is organized around getting through rather than living it.

What finally brought Moana to seek help was a recent moment in the hospital parking structure when the sight of two cars angled near each other brought back the accident so completely that she had to stop walking and grip the concrete pillar beside her. She was due to see patients within minutes and was shaken by how quickly her mind had been overtaken. She came in frightened that this is now permanent—that she has been changed irreversibly, that she cannot trust herself, and that danger is everywhere if she relaxes even briefly. At the same time, beneath her guardedness, she is hoping for something simple and profound: to be able to sleep without bracing, to sit in a room without calculating exits, and to remember what happened as something that occurred in her life rather than something that keeps happening to her.
